title: Language Access in Kidney and Dialysis Care
summary: Build language access into kidney education, dialysis training, transplant evaluation, medication counseling, teach-back, and follow-up.
body_markdown:
###


Begin when chronic kidney disease education and treatment choices are discussed, not only when dialysis starts. Continue through access planning, recurring dialysis, home training, transplant evaluation, medication changes, and follow-up.


###


Ask the patient to explain the plan in their own words while the interpreter conveys the response. For home procedures, use return demonstration. Document what the patient demonstrated or explained, what needed correction, and the follow-up plan.


###


Family members can support the patient, but they should not automatically replace a qualified interpretation pathway. Their language proficiency, health literacy, and role may be uncertain. Follow patient preference and organizational policy, and maintain access to an approved interpreter option.


###


Record the language and dialect when relevant, interpretation modality, major teaching topic, critical instructions, teach-back or return-demonstration result, unresolved questions, and any escalation. Use consistent EHR fields so the next team can continue the plan.


###


It can be used when approved by the organization and supported by safeguards, quality monitoring, patient preference, and a fallback. Confirm medications, numbers, dates, laterality, and other critical details. Human interpreters remain available according to policy and encounter needs.
